problem: A page can contain all the correct recognized characters while its transcription gives the wrong reading order or loses the page's row structure. The expected convention has to be fixed in the annotations.
example: With reference 牛奶 followed by a newline and 麵包, and predicted 麵包 followed by a newline and 牛奶, both strings contain four Chinese characters and one newline. Their multiset of characters matches, but their two-row order does not.
program: Counter counts occurrences without storing positions. The current prose explicitly says it includes the newline, which makes the later exercise easier to predict. == between Counters is True for the swapped rows; == between the exact strings is False. splitlines() preserves existing row sequence, returning [牛奶, 麵包] for reference and [麵包, 牛奶] for predicted. The imported standard-library function, two inputs and four printed results are explained by the text.
exercise: For predicted = 牛奶麵包, the four Chinese characters and their order are preserved, but the newline is absent and two rows become one. Counter equality and raw-string equality are False; splitlines() returns [牛奶麵包]. Removing all whitespace from both strings yields equality, which cannot certify the original row structure. A two-column receipt cannot have its intended reading order recovered from the four words alone; the page convention must say whether to continue down a column or cross both columns row by row.
numbers_and_symbols: The original strings each have four Chinese characters plus one newline and two rows. The no-newline variant has four characters and one row. == means equality comparison; \n encodes a newline. No mathematical formula appears in 20.11.
